124.t: Decca's poor sound versus RCA's Erskine Hawkins records
124.s: McRae fought with Decca over a bad-sounding Ella date after hearing Erskine Hawkins's "Tuxedo Junction" on RCA.
124.ch: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands

This is an all star date that he want to do for this thing (inaudible). He want to sell the records, because --…

124.t: The Decca "Where is the melody" sign and Chick Webb's drums
124.s: Decca's studio was cramped, with a sign asking for the melody that was covered whenever Webb's band recorded.
124.ch: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
124.q: Decca was a good studio, but they didn't have the space -- something they didn't have. They were going into this big band thing -- I know we were crowded in there when we did Chick Webb. We came off the road, the band was blowing like mad, you know, and they had to, "Hey, take it easy," you know.…

124.t: How studio dates were staffed and run in one take
124.s: Leaders hand-picked reliable men; they tuned up, ran each tune down once and recorded a single take, often without music.
124.ch: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
124.q: Like, if you were in New York, like they would call like the top musicians around to record. They'd pick certain guys that knew, you know, that they

124.t: Studio session length and ease of cutting four sides
124.s: Sessions ran about three hours and top musicians could do four sides easily.
124.ch: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
124.q: Well we never had any strains on us. We had a recording date -- Most of the time that we was recording, like ten o'clock or eleven o'clock -- whatever time we set -- most of the -- It was a usual thing, three hour day like they have now. You know, a session of three hours -- whatever the union call…

124.t: Calling the same top men; first-take dates
124.s: Leaders used reliable players like Cozy Cole, and McRae recalls running down keys and introductions and recording first takes.
124.ch: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
124.q: And like a lot of records that you have here -- that's in that book, in all these books -- some of these records we never heard.

124.t: Why leaders assembled special all-star players for dates
124.s: Teddy Wilson or Red Allen picked players for the sound they wanted rather than the men in their working bands.
124.ch: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
124.q: easy. See, because you see what happen was that the best thing about those dates were that all the musicians that were on the date, were all top musicians. And they all knew each other. And at one time had played a gig with each other -- a jam session with each other -- and they all played bands,…

124.s: Tape 3 begins; McRae continues comparing Decca and Brunswick studios with RCA's 23rd Street studio.
124.ch: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
124.q: Oh, (inaudible), yeah. Decca sound and the Brunswick sound too. You must remember that Decca -- those studios like that -- 50 West 52nd Street -- they didn't have the studios that RCA Victor had. RCA Victor had -- they only had down 23rd Street. That was considered one of the (inaudible) terrific…

124.s: McRae describes the padded, high-ceilinged RCA studio, where Fats Waller and many others recorded.
124.ch: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
124.q: : They had high ceilings. I don't know if they used asbestos then, but (inaudible) sounds were good. They were padded. Like they used a cloth padding or something in those days. The rugs on the floor was padded. The sounds were great. Because I know -- I did some dates down there (inaudible) some…

124.t: Recording from the middle of the studio floor
124.s: McRae sets balance by standing among the band instead of the control room, and cues the engineer.
124.q: And did "Moon Ray" the same thing. Just all head. That's what I'm saying. This is the difference between studio -- musicians and musicians that work in the studio all the time that's recording.

124.t: How recording dates and society gigs were staffed
124.s: Leaders like Red Allen or Teddy Wilson picked particular players for each date, so personnels changed from session to session.
124.ch: Rhythm Club, studio dates and the 1930s big bands
124.q: together (inaudible) talking about there. And we did some other gigs. We used to do hotel gigs together, like with different band leaders, you know. Guys like Snowden. Whoever got the gig together -- you know, whoever would come in. The call would come in and they had a gig, we would work for these…

63.t: Test cuts and listening back on bad speakers
63.s: He tested balance on a run-through, and had playbacks made boomy and quiet to hear what ordinary listeners would hear; discusses sound latitude.
63.q: We would make a test. Run it down for a test. Then I would listen to it. Then I’d say, all right. Now when we get back to letter C or letter B or number, bar so and so, you do this, you stand up, or you come down here, or brass do this, so and so. Another thing I did that was very different from…

63.t: How playbacks worked without acetates; the Interlude recording
63.s: Shaw cannot recall how playback worked before acetate or tape, and speculates about how the Interlude in B-flat second version got recorded.
63.q: Maybe there was some other thing that they had, or maybe a double . . . Yes, I think they had two turntables. One that you’d hear back, of the one you had just made. I’m pretty sure it was something like that. They put it on something, whatever it was. They didn’t have acetate. Whatever they had.…

63.t: Seasoning arrangements on the road before recording them
63.s: He rarely recorded an arrangement cold (Frenesi was the exception), preferring to play it on gigs first; four tunes were cut in a three-hour session.
63.q: Yeah. I tried to do that. I almost never did an arrangement in a studio the first time around. That was Frenesi. Studio musicians. We didn’t have the time . . . we didn’t get out on the road and play that piece enough. If we had, it would have loosened up and been a different record, but you…

63.t: Remaking Summertime; Stardust solos and the four-minute mile
63.s: After 22 takes of Summertime he re-recorded it at his own expense yet the wrong take was issued; he later had Ollie Wilson play the Jenney solo, likening it to breaking records.
63.q: At least 22. Finally, I chose one. Then the tapes came in . . . at that time, whatever they were. I had it home, and I played it and played it. I wasn’t happy with it. So at my own expense I took the band in and re-recorded it at what I considered the proper tempo and all that. Which one do you…

63.t: First overdubbing: playing clarinet to a recorded band on Love for Sale
63.s: A dental problem led him to add his part later through earphones to a recorded 44-piece band, an early dubbing.
63.ch: Billie Holiday, band members and singers
63.q: Oh, no no. That was studio work. Studio orchestras. Matter of fact, the first time an instrument was dubbed was in those sessions, on Love For Sale. I had to have some dental work done on the front of my mouth. I didn’t know it, but there was a tooth that had to be recapped. I didn’t know that at…

63.t: Editing Still's Chantais-les-bas and Lenox Avenue Blues; 12-inch records
63.s: Still's chart was too square so Shaw edited it and added ad libs, and he explains how long pieces like St. James Infirmary and Summertime needed 12-inch discs.
63.q: No. It was too stiff. A little too “square.” And the same thing with the blues, the Lenox Avenue Blues. We did a lot of ad libbing in that. That was a two-sided record. He wrote enough for about, oh, maybe four minutes, and I was going to do two sides. I had enough for three . . . almost seven…

454.t: Why live recording beats studio gimmicks
454.s: Live dates avoid gimmicks and retakes, but Atlantic dislikes them; the Showcase date recorded with the lights off.
454.q: They can only get what you're doing. And usually they do much better than what they would do with gimmicks.

454.t: Recording technology and engineers who read scores
454.s: Too many microphones and technology; an engineer should read the score, as Columbia engineers once did.
454.q: (Unintelligible) with Columbia Records, and Tio was there, he could read (inaudible).

454.t: Retyped pages: engineers and the ideal recording team
454.s: Repeat of engineers who read scores and Mingus's dream production team in Columbia's church studio.
454.q: I'd get Tio Becelle for engineer, (inaudible) written music. I'd get Les Paul for the engineer.

454.t: Studio atmosphere and an A&R man who stays in the booth
454.s: Mingus complains that his Atlantic A&R man cannot read scores or listen in the room; he brought Teo Macero in at his own cost.
454.q: He's got him, and couldn't read those scores, either, but this guy pretends to be a musician, and he can't read the scores. And he never comes out into the room to hear the sound of the music, musically.

454.t: His ideal recording team and setting
454.s: He would use Teddy Charles, Teo Macero and Les Paul and record in Columbia's church studio with unlimited time.
454.q: I'd get some guy who knows electronic things. I'd try to get the guy who's in Columbia.

454.s: Johnson contrasts Contemporary Records' open-ended sessions with East Coast practice.
454.ch: Teaching, race and the future of jazz
454.q: If they have some whisky, they bring it in. That's not the same as a guy (unintelligible) the beer.

61.t: Second masters and alternate takes in reissues
61.s: Alternate takes were marked -1/-2 or A/B; he issued strong ones as second masters but dislikes overlong alternate-take reissues.
61.ch: Hot Jazz Classics and how records were made
61.q: We just stopped for a bite of lunch. We were talking about the way records were made in the old pre-historic days of 1939, for example. This also relates to the second masters that I talked about, which were different takes than those that were issued. Sometimes, of course, two different takes got…

61.t: Splicing tape at Columbia and how masters became stampers
61.s: He defends splicing tape (Brubeck album) and explains the master, mother and stamper plating process.
61.ch: Hot Jazz Classics and how records were made
61.q: they buy it, they think to themselves, oh goodness, what a waste. I don’t really want all these breakdowns and so on. Sometimes there’s some very bad fluffs by the musicians, which is embarrassing. So I’ve always been very selective in that regard, and it has paid off. I’ll also jump ahead to a…

61.t: How early records were cut on wax by gravity-driven turntables
61.s: The wax cylinder, the falling stone, countdown starts and scraping failed takes.
61.ch: Hot Jazz Classics and how records were made
61.q: 77, but it was never exactly 78.6, or almost never exactly 78.6 in the old days. In fact, the standard I understand one time was something like 80, so that you’d hear music in the wrong keys. Even classic Armstrong records have been re-pitched as researchers have done what I never did, which was to…

61.s: The hot pressing room and hand finishing of each disc.
61.ch: Hot Jazz Classics and how records were made
61.q: in there with two labels, one for the bottom of the disc and one for the top, placed on spindles. The pressing would be literally pressed like that. As you watched this process – and the room was very hot, and it was kind of odorous, because you had all the smells of this compound as well as heat…

371.t: Not the Savoy house pianist; why Van Gelder's studio drew everyone
371.s: Jones says the Savoy dates were a cycle, and that engineers draw artists; Van Gelder recorded for Blue Note, Prestige and others.
371.q: No, not really. I think everything goes in cycles. You know, we did all those dates and back happened to be the cycle that we were in another time. They were doing a lot of recordings. I guess, I was lucky enough to get the call and some of them. I enjoyed working there. I really enjoyed working on…

371.t: Rudy Van Gelder and his Steinway B
371.s: Van Gelder was fiercely protective of his piano, which was the finest Jones ever played; he preferred the home studio sound.
371.q: (Laughs) You don’t want to know! Well, Van Gelder was very particular about the piano. I cannot fault him for that because he had one of the greatest recording instruments I have ever heard, or that I was ever fortunate enough to play on. He had a Steinway B in his studio that had no equal. It had…

371.t: A&R men Ozzie Cadena and Teddy Reig, sweetening dates, no rehearsals
371.s: Cadena and Reig understood the music; Jones also did sweetening dates; sessions had no rehearsals.
371.q: I will say that Ozzy Cadena was the one who was…I think… You work tomorrow closely with him. He seemed to have a greater affinity for the music. Although, he himself was not a musician, he seems to know what he wanted. Teddy Reid was also very good at that. Teddy Reid was an A&R man for, I think it…

371.t: More 1955 sessions, Marlene VerPlanck, and the unforgettable piano
371.s: Date after date, a vocal session, a solo album, and again Jones recalls the Van Gelder piano.
371.ch: 1950s clubs, Savoy dates and the Detroit sound
371.q: Well, even then…Let’s see was it Ver Plank? Yes, she was married to Billy Ver Plank, a pianist and arranger. I was playing a gig with them, I guess a couple years ago.

9.t: Acoustic recording horns and the day-long 'I Can't Give You Anything But Love' with Armstr
9.s: Early recording used horns, and the Louis Armstrong date spent half a day on a single melody-backing number before 'Mahogany Hall Stomp' the next day.
9.q: : Oh yeah. Sure. Of course, in them days, there was not the high fidelity that they have nowadays, you know what I mean, in recording...

9.t: Daytime sessions with no rehearsal and little interest in records
9.s: Sessions were mostly daytime, tunes were often handed out in the studio without arrangements, and records were just a means of survival.
9.q: : No, it was mostly in the daytime. Definitely. They were from 9 o'clock in the morning til noon, or from noon until 5 o'clock or something like that. It was strictly daytime recording.

9.t: Recording under three minutes and Russell's arranging
9.s: Numbers rehearsed on the job had to be cut to under three minutes for records, with Russell arranging and many head numbers.
9.ch: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
9.q: playing... See, while we was on the job working... You know, like, when we was workin' in a club a nightclub or something, boy, we rehearsed...we played the numbers during the night, and be rehearsing them while we're playing them. Then when we get to the studio, we'd know what we're doing. But…

9.t: 'I Can't Give You Anything But Love' with no arrangement
9.s: With no arrangement and a three-minute limit, the technicians held all the say and the whole session produced one side.
9.ch: Russell's band, records and Armstrong in the studio
9.q: Oh, no. There was no arrangement. I mean, there was nothing written out for it. They had no music whatsoever. The first thing, they had to get the time on the thing. It had to be under three minutes. So they had to figure how many choruses, how many interludes, bars you could put in there to fill…

387.s: The difference between live and mechanical recordings.
387.q: It's very easy to tell if you AB it with something that has a live thing about it, where they're truly interacting. If they're just reading notes

387.t: Overdubbed telephoned parts versus live sessions
387.s: He objects to dead recordings made without interaction.
387.q: they don't do anymore. Now everybody telephones his part, which is a terrible thing. It drives me insane. It makes for a lifeless recording.

387.t: Dead studios versus the live sound
387.s: Studio padding made records sound thin; live bands filled the room unamplified.
387.q: They were all recorded in that fashion in those days, and I think that is one of the reasons they sound that way. I don't think they materially sounded different from the way a band sounds

387.t: Recording at Victor's studio and the sound
387.s: Hearing the band for the first time in a union hall studio.
387.q: when we heard the band, and it was at a good place, on 34th Street, Victor had a union hall next to the hotel, west of Eighth Avenue--I forgot what the name of the place was, but it had a good ring to it. They used to do the NBC symphony broadcast from there too. It was a union hall.

10.t: Sound quality and speed of the Morton acetates
10.s: They talk about the primitive equipment, clicking heels, and the pitch of Morton's voice on different reissues.
10.q: they used a little uh uh antique i i think i don't think the equipment was of the highest order they have very good equipment today but in those days uh i don't know what they had to tell you the truth

10.t: Morton's singing and spontaneity in the studio
10.s: Morton surprised people by singing on the records, and never played a piece the same way twice.
10.q: He laughed one time, he said he'd gotten a letter from some woman that bought, liked his records, and she says, I like your singing. And he says to me, he says, that's funny. He says, how hard they did any singing on any of them. How funny she liked to sing. But he did shout out once in a while…

10.t: Morton's Washington sessions at United Recording and the Jazzman issues
10.s: Where Morton recorded in Washington, how the Jazzman and Vogue issues came about without the engineer knowing, and Carew getting Morton to join the union.
10.q: Well, it was on 9th Street there. If you remember where the old Greenwall Theater used to be, just above G Street. There was a moving picture house just above G Street. And I think it was right next door to where that was. I'm a little hazy on when they demolished the old theater, but there was a…

41.t: Recording George Lewis and using radio studios
41.s: Mares recorded Lewis at WDSU and used WTPS and WSMB, choosing rooms for sound.
41.q: Ah, yes, I recorded George at WDSU, and I got a real nice recording of George, and like I said, done in the studio, and we took time out to tune up.

41.t: The Tom Brown session and his demands
41.s: Tom Brown's session was done at WDSU after rehearsals at the studio; he first wanted conditions but tore up his list after talking with Mares.
41.q: Yeah, we always put the session together here, we map out and we get our patterns here, who's going to play this and what's what, and go over the tunes, and exchange a few ideas. I have my own ideas what I want, but I always like to hear things and suggestions, and we always put them together and…

41.t: Which Southland albums were made where
41.s: Mares lists sessions made in the studio, at Woodman Hall, WDSU and other spots.
41.q: Well, I did the Sharky with these Kings of Dixieland, and I call it the Sharky and the Jam Session in New Orleans here. That's my 205, and I made it right here in the studio. We have some live applause there, which naturally I added to it. And I've done the Monk Hazel Session in here. That's the…

22.t: Recording for Columbia and Victor, and acoustic recording methods
22.s: He describes the failed Columbia session, the Victor sessions with an eight-inch horn, and how many takes were cut.
22.q: Max Hart fixed a date for us to go up there and make a record Now this place was located at 16 Broadway It was only a block away from Rides and Rambus We went up there one morning to record And they told us to play over the piece And when they did that They were all putting their hands to their…

22.t: Aeolian Vocalion records and who played on them
22.s: He explains the move to Aeolian over royalties, the playback incompatibility, and the lineup on the New York records.

We thought that they'd play on any machine. And we went over there on a royalty basis. That'd give us two cents a…

22.t: Tiger Rag recording conditions, Kid Ory comparison and W.C. Handy's record
22.s: He compares a recent Ory record with the 1918 Tiger Rag, describes acoustic recording setup, and plays a Handy Columbia record while disputing Handy's claims.
22.ch: Records and the claim that Black bands copied
22.q: Playing a tiger rag. This is Dixonland Jubilee by Kit Ory. This is only about a year old. Between this and the one that I'll play that was played almost 42 years ago, 41 years ago, you'll see the difference. That's what these white men call good music. Some of these tribes should go back in Africa…

8.t: Recording horn setup and band placement
8.s: Everyone played into one horn, with the band arranged around it; no one moved.
8.q: Yeah. Did you face it? Do you remember how you were? Yeah, I remember good enough and nice day. Well, tell me how it was. I missed it.

8.s: No retakes; they rehearsed beforehand and played each number straight through.
8.q: We didn't, we didn't lose no time at all. You just went and played it, like when you made the orange curl trombone. You just play it once? We didn't have just played like we generally do play it and then, all right, let's cut, let's try this and over.

8.t: Acoustic recording: drums, bass and personnel
8.s: In the small studio, drums and bass did not record; the drummer used woodblock and cymbal. Singers and personnel are listed.
8.q: Something like this room here. Little old place. Small room, huh? Yeah. Little old place, you know. And we went out there and at that time making those records the drums didn't take, bass didn't take. And making them records the drummer had to take like this thing here and set a cymbal on his…

1034.t: Overdubs, three-take limit and the red recording light
1034.s: He captured spontaneity with a rundown and at most three takes, and describes players freezing when the red light came on.
1034.q: Oh I went through that, but most of the producers, when I was a session player, most of the producers I worked with luckily were great producers, and they knew to cut and capture the spontaneity. That’s what I always tried to do. That’s why when I was starting out as a producer I knew when they…

1034.t: Rhythm tracks, scratch vocals and playing live off the floor
1034.s: Artists were present for rhythm tracks with scratch vocals; he compares Motown crowding, headphones, live strings and direct-to-disc pressure.
1034.q: Yes. If it wasn’t the artist there would be somebody in there, they called it, “the scratch vocal.” Usually the artist was there. I can think of only a few occasions if something happened and we had to cut a track without the artist being there. The artist was always there. Anywhere. On either…

1034.s: He recalls recording on four, eight, sixteen and twenty-four tracks and the cost of giant consoles and vintage microphones.
1034.q: guys. You’ve got to know the tech — and back then the technical part — like I was telling this class today here, the recording class, you know we recorded on this giant analog consoles, which are still the best. Well when I first started it was four track, then we went to George Massenburg and I…

539.t: George Martin, Spector and the glue of making records
539.s: Dorn gives his view of George Martin and explains how Spector and Lieber and Stoller records combine overtones, echo and the moment. He says he is a record producer, not a jazz producer.
539.q: It’s not bad work it’s just that combination of the five of them. You’re not going to get that again certainly in this epoch.

539.t: Why live and club recordings differ and getting Les McCann to love the studio
539.s: Dorn says a good live record captures a moment. He fixed Les McCann's dislike of the studio with a second tape machine so the tape never stopped.
539.q: The second you say we’re recording live — I made a lot of live records, most of them were not successful. When I say not successful, they didn’t become gigantic live recordings you know. Like Cannonball at the Jazz Workshop or Horace at the Village Gate or you know, Ramsey at the Bohemian Caverns,…

539.t: Technology: two linked 16-track machines and mixing with Gene Paul
539.s: Dorn claims to be first to link two 16-track machines. He describes his current studio with Gene Paul and mixing analog and digital.
539.q: I invented more tracks. And I’m going to tell you the one thing I did that had to do with technology. I was the first person to hook two 16-track tape machines together. Because sometimes I was so nuts there were just never enough tracks.

964.t: Hands-on in a small studio and knowing when a song is done
964.s: Gold's first Neve console and 24-track room, selling the studio, and letting his engineer finish mixes.
964.q: Well as I just said before this record business and the film business is based on technology. So what happens is things keep getting bigger, more complicated, it's just big. My first Neve I had was 15 channels. About this big. It was an old broadcast board. That was amazing, that I could line…

964.s: Gold describes big tape reels and how overdubbing meant bouncing between tape recorders in the early 1960s.
964.q: That's a big reel too. Usually they weren't quite that big. That's almost double the amount of tape. Usually they were half that size but that wide. Yeah I mean, hey look, those days were special in lots and lots of different ways because a lot of that stuff was just being invented in a way too. It…

964.t: String section size, speakers and Sigma studio
964.s: Gold's typical section, doubling against union rules, recording without headphones in the 1960s, and Phil Ramone's surprise at small Sigma.
964.q: Well it all depends. In the old days I had six violins, two violas, and two cellos, which I still do a lot today. And much against union rules, I double that. And even back in the '70s and the '60s I used to double that. So, and that to me, if I get a couple of great performances that's plenty.

994.t: Studio footage, headphones and in-ear monitors
994.s: Rowe asks about a documentary clip of the drummer without headphones; Scales says it was likely B-roll or in-ears.
994.q: So if it was from the studio and it was footage it could be that he was just playing and that it wasn’t being recorded right then for the album. More than likely. It could have been just like B-roll.

994.t: Choosing and editing takes as a producer
994.s: He picks takes that best present the composition, splices takes freely, and ensures the band can play it live.
994.q: There’s an art to that. And I feel like you can’t tell with my stuff either you know? But part of that is because we play well together and we know how each other works so like there’s like a magic that happens behind the scenes that allows me to create the recorded music in the way that I do as a…

994.s: He makes household-object demos and gives players written parts, chords and time signatures.
994.q: It’s a combination of all that. So sometimes I’ll make like a demo in my own bastardized way. Like I would make these drum tracks sometimes where I would just like pick up random household objects and I’ll play the kick drum part on like a pillow and record it, like hitting the stick with a pillow…

165.t: Singing around one microphone and objections to isolation booths
165.s: He prefers close proximity to isolation, recounting a Brubeck session, and criticizes engineers.
165.ch: Vocalese and Lambert, Hendricks and Ross
165.q: No, because you can’t hear what the other person’s singing, so you lose the blend. Whatever blend you attain comes from the engineer. I think it should come from the singers. I don’t agree with a lot of modern recording technique. I think it’s good for the record companies, but it’s not good for…

165.t: Sing a Song of Basie changed how singers are recorded
165.s: He says the album changed how jazz is sung, introduced multitracking, and printed lyrics on the back.
165.ch: Vocalese and Lambert, Hendricks and Ross
165.q: It turns out that it was not just a breakthrough for us, but even, forgetting who did it, forgetting that I was involved in that or that I had anything to do with that – looking at that as an artistic piece of work, it changed the way jazz music is sung. It changed the way people record singers.

165.t: How the multitracking of Basie parts was done
165.s: With four tracks, they layered voices three at a time and recorded the lead last, using the Basie rhythm section tape.
165.ch: Vocalese and Lambert, Hendricks and Ross
165.q: It worked then very primitively, because they had no 24-track – not even 12 tracks, not even 8 tracks. There were only 4. So what we had to do was pile everything on a master tape. Like we would record we three singing, and then on top – then we would record another tape of we three singing…

460.t: Rudy Van Gelder's flute sound compared with Atlantic engineers
460.s: Laws praises Rudy Van Gelder for capturing the flute better than anyone, contrasts engineers at Atlantic, and mentions Phil Ramone and Van Gelder's white gloves.
460.ch: Studio work, Rudy Van Gelder and Freddie Hubbard
460.q: When I was with Atlantic Records, the engineers, they looked at the dials a lot, and they’d look at the display rather than really try to capture the sound of the instrument. Rudy, on the other hand – I think it’s like anything else. You have the best when it comes to doctors, lawyers, cooks,…

460.s: Laws describes the close single Shure mic on his mouthpiece, the isolation booth, and Van Gelder's secrecy about equipment.
460.ch: Studio work, Rudy Van Gelder and Freddie Hubbard
460.q: It was a Shure mic, just a boom Shure, and it put one of those – a wind screen over it. But it’s not so much that as what he did with the dials on the consol.

460.t: Rudy's bluntness, Creed's diplomacy and consoling Rudy
460.s: Laws recalls Rudy Van Gelder shutting down a session over a visiting engineer, contrasts him with Creed Taylor, and recalls consoling him after his wife died.

72.t: Recording technology: Victor with Oliver versus Blue Note
72.s: With Oliver his drums were muffled with a handkerchief and partitions; Blue Note let him play freely.
72.ch: Art Hodes, Bechet and Blue Note

412.t: The 1942 Decca date at nine in the morning
412.s: Hodes tells how a fan's father got him a Decca date through Dave Kapp. The only slot offered was 9 a.m., and the engineers set up the studio badly. He says it was still one of his best dates.
412.ch: Wingy Manone and Bix in Chicago (draft typing)
412.q: And you don't drag yourself like that. And a good example of that was getting up at 9:00 in the morning, because that's the only time Decca would give us to make a date in 1942.

95.t: How a recording session worked at Okeh
95.s: She describes rehearsing, timing, making two takes and the wax on the studio floor, taking two to three hours.

239.t: Conducting a Johnny Hodges date at 9 a.m. on a Monday
239.s: Jones called a morning session on 42nd Street with a strong band and hung up a joke sign to loosen everybody.
239.ch: Recording dates, Goodman and band life
239.q: I called this date, the first date, at 9:00 o'clock in the morning, because -- on a Monday, because psychologically if the guys have been off on the weekend they might be hanging over a little bit.

112.t: First recordings in Berlin through acoustic horns
112.s: The recording people came after four or five days; the drums were placed in the hall and the band played into horns, recording show numbers.
112.q: : First wasn't Polydor. Anyhow, we had been there about four or five days and then come the people from the recording company, and said, 'Look, we would like for you to record.'
